newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada asks Supreme Court ruling on Quebec separation.
newsitem.headline: Canada asks Supreme Court ruling on Quebec separation.

text.p: Canadian Justice Minister Allan Rock on Thursday said he would ask the country's Supreme Court to rule on the legality of any future unilateral declaration of independence by French-speaking Quebec.

Following a razor-thin victory for federalists in last October's referendum on Quebec separation, the Liberal government's action was seen as a bid to set clear rules on who gets the final word in any future vote on independence.
Quebec reacted dismissively to Ottawa's latest move.
"There is only one court that can decide the political future of Quebec. It is, of course, in Quebec, by the people of Quebec," the province's premier Lucien Bouchard told reporters in Quebec City.

Bouchard's separatist goverment has argued that Quebec people alone have the right to chose whether to keep their province in Canada, but Rock on Thursday said this view contradicted both Canada's constitution and international law.
"In our view, that position is contrary to Canadian law, is unsupported by international law and is deeply threatening to the orderly governance of our land," Rock told parliament.

He said the government would seek a Supreme Court ruling on whether a unilateral declaration of independence by the Quebec government is legal under Canada's constitution and international law and whether domestic or international law would take precedence in Canada if there is a conflict.

"The government of Canada does not argue against the legitimacy of a consultative referendum," Rock said. "But however important that consultation may be, the result of a referendum does not, in and of itself, effect legal change."

The Liberal government's failure to take more decisive measures against a possible split attracted severe criticism after separatists came within one percentage point of winning the October referendum.
Bouchard discarded Ottawa's decision and said a Supreme Court ruling would have no impact on future referendums on Quebec sovereignty.
"It is certain that it will not affect in any way the future of Quebec and the determination of this government to hold a referendum," he told Quebec City reporters in French.
Asked whether Ottawa's action would affect his "referendum calendar," Bouchard replied: "Not at all," adding that he would continue focusing on Quebec's economic woes.
Rock's announcement was also met with outrage by the separatist Bloc Quebecois, which holds official opposition status in Canada's Parliament.

"Now that it is afraid of losing, the federal goverment is trying to throw doubt on the entire Quebec referendum process, and to impose its own referendum rules," Bloc Quebecois deputy Pierrette Venne said in response to Rock's announcement.

Ottawa's appeal to the Supreme Court would be separate from Quebec lawyer Guy Bertrand's court battle against separation. The former separatist was mulling whether to continue with his demand before a Quebec Superior Court judge for an injunction against any future sovereignty referendums that would lead to a unilateral declaration of independence.

In a move that sparked outrage in Quebec City, the federal government backed Bertrand's case in court, arguing that the Canadian constitution and the courts should have a role to play in any Quebec secession process. Quebec's lawyers argued that Quebec voters alone can decide their political future through a democratic vote in a referendum.

Under Quebec law, the separatist government cannot hold another sovereignty referendum until after the next Quebec election. That is to be called at the provincial premier's discretion and could be up to three years away.
